name: Goldpaster
tagline: A desktop paste utility: clipboard history, saved snippets, and fast keyboard recall.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Clipboard history is one of the most one-shot-able categories in software: a background listener, a local database, a search box, and a global hotkey. An agent can get you a working local version in a single session, and the data never needs to leave your machine, which is arguably better for a tool that sees every password you copy. The honest caveat is that we know very little about this particular product, so if it does something unusual with cross-device sync, rich formats, or team snippet libraries, the gap widens. Polish is where paid clipboard tools earn their keep: hotkey conflicts, paste-as-plain-text, pinned items, and not leaking memory while sitting in your menu bar for three weeks. Build it, run it for a month, and you will know exactly which of those you actually missed.
coreLoopDIY: Watches the system clipboard, stores every text and image copy in a local SQLite database, and brings up a searchable overlay on a global hotkey that pastes the chosen entry back into the focused app.
requirements: macOS or Windows dev machine with Node and the Rust toolchain
Accessibility or input monitoring permission granted to the dev build
Optional code signing if you want it to launch without warnings on other machines
whatYouLose: Cross-device sync, so your phone and second laptop keep their own separate histories
A signed, notarized, auto-updating binary instead of a dev build you rebuild by hand
Handling for the weird clipboard flavors: rich text, file references, images from specific apps
Years of accumulated hotkey and focus-stealing edge cases that only show up in real use
Someone else to blame when it silently stops recording copies
moatNotes: Clipboard tools get sticky because the history itself becomes a working memory you do not want to abandon, not because the code is hard.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a clipboard manager is infrastructure you touch forty times a day, and infrastructure that glitches is worse than no infrastructure at all. Paid tools in this space are selling reliability, a menu bar presence that never hangs, sane defaults for paste-as-plain-text, and the fact that someone else tested it against the OS update that broke everything. A weekend build gets you ninety percent of the function and none of that assurance, which is a fine trade for a personal tool and a bad one for a team.
notes: Public details on this one are thin, so treat the verdict as category-level rather than product-level.
prompt:
Build a local clipboard manager desktop app. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Tauri v2 with a React plus TypeScript frontend, Vite for the dev server
- Rust backend using the tauri clipboard-manager and global-shortcut plugins
- SQLite via tauri-plugin-sql for storage, file lives in the app data directory
- Tailwind for styling, no component library

Core behavior:
- A Rust background task polls the system clipboard every 400ms and writes new text entries to SQLite with content, a sha256 hash, char count, source app name if available, and a created_at timestamp
- Deduplicate on hash: if the incoming item matches the newest row, do nothing; if it matches an older row, bump that row to the top instead of inserting
- Also capture images as PNG blobs on disk with a row pointing at the file path
- Global hotkey Cmd+Shift+V (Ctrl+Shift+V on Windows) opens a frameless, always-on-top, 640px wide overlay window centered on the active display
- The overlay is a search box plus a keyboard-navigable list of the last 500 entries, fuzzy filtered as you type, arrow keys to move, Enter to paste, Escape to close
- Enter writes the entry back to the clipboard, hides the overlay, then synthesizes a paste keystroke into the previously focused app
- Shift+Enter pastes as plain text with whitespace trimmed
- Cmd+P on a highlighted row pins it; pinned rows sort above everything else and are never pruned
- Settings screen: history limit, poll interval, launch at login toggle, and a list of app bundle ids to ignore so password managers are never recorded
- A Clear history button that actually vacuums the database

Explicitly out of scope: sync, mobile, sharing, snippet variables, OCR, any network call whatsoever.

Deliverables: working dev build via npm run tauri dev, a README with the hotkey list and the permissions macOS will prompt for, and a seed script that inserts 50 fake entries so the list can be tested without copying things by hand. Keep all config in .env where secrets would otherwise be needed; there should be none.
